Cover StoryThe flexible-dieting question

Why Can Some People Stay Shredded While Eating Pizza, Burgers and Ice Cream?

The secret usually isn't a magical metabolism—or a food that burns fat. It's the bigger picture: energy balance, daily movement, training, protein, portions and a routine someone can actually sustain.

Fitness Science Desk · Sponsored editorial for Edgefit.appResearch reviewed: November 2026

A flexible approach can make room for favorite foods while keeping the overall plan aligned with personal goals. Editorial illustration.

You've seen it: someone finishes a burger and fries, grabs a slice of pizza later, and still looks lean year-round. Meanwhile, another person weighs every almond, avoids every dessert and struggles to see the same definition. So what gives?

The easy explanation is “genetics.” Genetics do matter—but the full story is more useful. People differ in body size, appetite, spontaneous movement, training volume, food preferences and how much energy they consume across an entire week. Someone who appears to eat anything may simply eat smaller portions at other meals, move more throughout the day, or naturally regulate intake without tracking it.

And a single meal tells you almost nothing about someone's long-term energy balance. Body composition reflects patterns over time, not whether a person ate pizza on Friday night.

The real freedom isn't eating without limits. It's learning how to include the foods you enjoy while keeping the bigger plan on track.

The “secret” is usually a system—not a cheat food

There is no credible evidence that pizza, burgers or ice cream independently trigger fat loss. But favorite foods do not automatically cancel progress either. When total intake is appropriate for the goal, a flexible eating pattern can include a wide range of foods.

Energy balanceBody-weight change is shaped by the relationship between energy intake and expenditure, with biology and environment influencing both sides.
Protein priorityAdequate protein can support satiety and help preserve lean mass during a calorie-restricted phase.
Daily movementWalking, work, errands and other non-exercise activity can meaningfully affect total daily energy expenditure.
ConsistencyA plan that can be repeated is often more useful than a perfect plan abandoned after two weeks.

What peer-reviewed research actually says

Several studies support a more flexible, evidence-informed approach—but each has limits. Here is what the research can reasonably support, and what it cannot prove.

Randomized controlled trial · 2021

Flexible vs. rigid dieting in resistance-trained individuals

Conlin and colleagues studied 23 resistance-trained adults over a 20-week protocol. During the 10-week calorie-restricted phase, both groups reduced body weight and fat mass; there were no significant between-group differences. This supports flexibility as a viable option—not a claim that food choice never matters.

Journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, 18, 52.

Read the clinical trial ↗
Dietary restraint validation · 1999

Flexible and rigid control of eating behavior

Westenhoefer, Stunkard and Pudel analyzed questionnaire and food-diary data from 54,517 participants in a weight-reduction program, plus validation samples. Flexible control was associated with lower disinhibition and a higher probability of successful weight reduction during the program. This was observational/validation research, not a randomized comparison of diet plans.

Journal: International Journal of Eating Disorders, 26(1), 53–64.

Read the paper ↗
Scientific review · 2022

The energy balance model of obesity: beyond calories in, calories out

Hall and colleagues explain energy balance as a biological system involving the brain, hormones, nervous-system signals, food environment and energy needs. The paper discusses evidence from many studies, including a cited network meta-analysis of 121 trials; it is not itself a 121-trial meta-analysis.

Journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 115(5), 1243–1254.

Read the review ↗
Clinical evidence review · 2020

Clinical evidence and mechanisms of high-protein diet-induced weight loss

Moon and Koh review clinical evidence that higher-protein diets can reduce fat mass while helping preserve fat-free mass in some weight-loss settings. Protein needs vary, and more is not automatically better for every person.

Journal: Journal of Obesity & Metabolic Syndrome, 29(3), 166–173.

Read the review ↗
Systematic review · 2021

Self-monitoring via digital health in weight-loss interventions

Patel and colleagues reviewed digital self-monitoring in behavioral weight-loss interventions. The evidence connects engagement with digital monitoring to weight-loss outcomes; it does not prove that one app, AI food photo feature or macro logger is inherently more accurate than manual tracking.

Journal: Obesity, 29(3), 478–499.

Read the systematic review ↗
Research integrity note: A purported 2026 “Calorie Tracking App Accuracy” meta-analysis and the quoted 5.1% protein / 6.3% carbohydrate error figures could not be independently verified as a credible peer-reviewed journal publication. They are not used to substantiate Edgefit's capabilities or accuracy. The Stanford Medicine article is a news summary of a systematic review—not evidence that Edgefit's AI tools produce a specific weight-loss result.

So how do you build a flexible plan that still works?

Start with a realistic calorie range for your goal, establish a sensible protein target, build meals around foods you enjoy, and keep resistance training progressive. Use trend data rather than judging progress by one weigh-in. Adjust gradually when the pattern—not a single day—shows that the plan needs changing.

01 · Set the target

Use a practical calorie and macro framework rather than banning entire food groups without a reason.

02 · Train with intent

Organize strength work, progression and recovery around your actual schedule.

03 · Track the pattern

Review workouts, body metrics and food choices over time; use the feedback to make small adjustments.

Energy Balance Beats Food Moralizing

For decades, mainstream diet culture sorted foods into two rigid buckets: “clean” foods that shrink your waist and “cheat” foods that instantly derail fat loss. Yet human metabolism does not read ingredient labels with moral judgment. Body fat changes are governed first and foremost by sustained energy balance—the relationship between total calories consumed and total calories expended over weeks and months.

When someone stays lean while enjoying two slices of pepperoni pizza on Friday night or a scoop of ice cream after dinner, they are not breaking the laws of thermodynamics. They are accounting for those calories inside a controlled daily or weekly budget while anchoring the rest of their intake around high-protein, nutrient-dense meals.

“A diet you can follow at 85% consistency for a year will outperform a ‘perfect’ chicken-and-broccoli plan you abandon every third weekend.”
Pillar 01 · Caloric Awareness

Guessing portions on high-calorie foods can hide 400–700 extra kcal. Instant tracking turns guesswork into clearer numbers.

Pillar 02 · Protein Protection

Hitting daily protein targets helps preserve lean muscle tissue during a deficit and can support appetite management.

Pillar 03 · Zero Binge Triggers

Removing rigid “off-limits” rules can help prevent the restrict-and-binge cycle that derails many fat-loss attempts.

Why Traditional Macro Tracking Fails Real People

Knowing that flexible dieting can work is one thing; executing it in the middle of a busy workday or at a restaurant table is another. Traditional calorie apps can force users to search databases, weigh every garnish and manually enter multiple ingredients for a single meal. Logging fatigue can set in—and once tracking stops, calorie creep can quietly return.

AI nutrition tools aim to reduce that adherence bottleneck by making meal logging faster and simpler. Edgefit brings several logging methods into one workflow, so users can choose the one that fits the moment.

The Edgefit approach: structure without food fear

Edgefit is not a metabolic shortcut, a medical treatment or a promise that you can eat without limits. It is a practical system for organizing training, nutrition targets and progress data—so a flexible approach has a better chance of becoming a consistent routine.

The bottom line

People who stay lean while eating a broad range of foods are not necessarily breaking the rules. They may have found a balance between what they eat, how much they move, how they train and what they can sustain. Flexible dieting is not a loophole in energy balance. It is one way to make a nutrition plan livable.
